title: 11+ English: How to Improve Comprehension, Inference and Vocabulary
description: Practical 11+ English guidance on comprehension, inference, vocabulary, accurate answers and reviewing mistakes, for entrance tests that include English.

children: Build the Reading Skills the Test Requires

Where an 11+ entrance test includes English, strong performance depends on more than completing lots of practice papers. Children need secure reading habits, precise vocabulary and a method for turning evidence from a text into clear answers. The exact format still depends on the school or local test, so use its official guidance alongside these core skills.
Read the whole passage for sense:
establish the situation, sequence and overall tone before answering detailed questions.
Underline evidence:
make the child show which word, phrase or sentence supports an answer.
Paraphrase accurately:
practise expressing an idea in different words without changing its meaning.
Check against the question:
confirm that every part of the answer is relevant to what was actually asked.

The purpose of practice is to make the reading process more deliberate. A child should gradually become better at finding evidence, explaining what it implies and checking whether an answer really matches the question.
Comprehension: Read for Meaning Before Hunting for Answers

A common weakness is rushing straight to the questions and scanning for matching words. Strong comprehension starts with understanding what is happening, who is involved, what changes and what the writer is suggesting.
Retrieval:
locate explicit facts and details accurately.
Inference:
use textual clues to reach a justified conclusion.
Explanation:
connect evidence to the idea clearly rather than copying a quotation and stopping.
These skills are best taught through discussion first, then short written answers. Asking a child to explain why an answer is right often reveals more than simply marking it correct or incorrect.
Inference: Move from Evidence to a Justified Idea

Inference questions ask children to work out something that is suggested rather than stated directly. The answer still needs evidence: an inference should be the most reasonable explanation of the details in the text, not a guess based on personal opinion.
Find the clue:
identify the exact detail that suggests something beyond the literal statement.
State the inference:
explain what that clue reasonably tells you about a character, situation or attitude.
Test the idea:
check that the inference fits the rest of the passage and does not contradict other evidence.
A useful teaching sequence is evidence first, inference second, explanation third. If a child cannot point to the detail that supports the idea, the inference probably needs reconsidering.

Vocabulary: Learn Words in Context

Large vocabulary lists can create the illusion of progress. It is more useful to meet unfamiliar words in reading, infer meaning from context, discuss roots and related words, and then reuse the vocabulary in speech or writing.
Infer from context:
use nearby words and the wider sentence before reaching for a dictionary.
Explore word families:
connect roots, prefixes, suffixes, synonyms and antonyms.
Notice precise differences:
discuss why two near-synonyms are not always interchangeable.
Reuse new vocabulary:
apply the word in a new sentence so meaning becomes active rather than passive.
Repeated exposure matters. A word becomes useful when a child can recognise it in a new sentence and understand the shade of meaning, not merely recall a flashcard definition once.
Accuracy: Answer the Question That Was Asked

Many lost marks come from imprecise reading of the question rather than lack of ability. Train children to notice command words, line references, how many points are required and whether the question wants retrieval, inference, explanation or comparison.
Circle the command word:
identify whether the task asks you to find, explain, infer, compare or give evidence.
Respect the line range:
do not use evidence from outside the section named in the question.
Match the number of points:
if two reasons are required, make sure two distinct reasons are actually given.
Check every claim:
remove ideas that cannot be supported by the passage.
A short, accurate answer is often stronger than a long response containing several unsupported ideas. Precision should come before length.

Use Practice Papers as Diagnosis, Not Just Scores
Practice papers become much more useful when every mistake is classified. Instead of recording only a percentage, identify what caused each error and make the next practice task address that cause.
Knowledge gap:
the child did not know a word, grammar point or underlying concept.
Reading error:
an important word, line reference or detail was missed or misread.
Reasoning error:
the evidence was found but the conclusion did not follow from it.
Technique error:
the child knew the answer but lost accuracy through timing, careless selection or poor checking.
This turns a paper into a teaching tool. If several errors come from vocabulary, the next step is not necessarily another full paper; it may be targeted reading and word work.
How to Review an 11+ English Mistake
After a wrong answer, ask the child to reconstruct the thinking rather than simply reveal the correct option. That creates a repeatable process for improvement.
What did the question require?
Restate it in simple terms.
What evidence should have led to the answer?
Find and underline it.
What will you do differently next time?
Write one specific rule or reminder and then try a similar question.
Over time, the error log should show fewer repeated mistakes and more independent correction. That is more informative than one isolated high or low practice score.
A Simple Weekly English Routine

A sustainable routine might combine regular reading, short vocabulary work, one focused comprehension task and deliberate review of previous errors. Add timed work gradually when the child is secure enough for speed to be a useful challenge rather than a source of random mistakes.
